title: Katherine Mansfield, The Garden Party recast
author: Salon
note: A Sarrià lawn, a marquee, and leftovers carried down to a death the party refused to see. After Mansfield, The Garden Party, 1922.

scenes.title: The lawn above Sarrià
scenes.reentry: They were still deciding where the marquee should go when the morning already smelled of cut grass and coffee from the kitchen terrace.

breaths.text: They were still deciding where the marquee should go when the morning already smelled of cut grass and coffee from the kitchen terrace.

The Serra house sat above Sarrià like a pale ship: white shutters, a lemon tree that had survived three renovations, a view that slid down through pines toward the city haze and, beyond it, a strip of Mediterranean that looked invented.

Laura loved mornings like this—the workmen’s Spanish and Catalan mixed, the thump of tent poles, her mother’s voice floating from an upstairs window as if the day were a score she alone could conduct.
“Not against the karaka,” José called, meaning the old citrus.
“Against the corner, where the light is flatter.”
José was practical in linen.
Núria was still in her silk kimono, eating a peach over the sink so the juice would not ruin anything important.

Jordi, home from a week of remote work that was not quite work, took the front steps two at a time and kissed Laura’s cheek with the affectionate violence of brothers who still believed the house belonged to all of them equally.
Laura went down to the lawn because someone had to speak to the men as if they were guests.
She was twenty and soft-spoken and certain, in the way of people who have never yet been contradicted by grief, that kindness was a language everyone shared.
The tallest workman had a cigarette behind his ear and eyes that did not flatter her.
She felt, briefly, ridiculous in her hat.
Then he smiled—only a little—and the ridiculousness became something warmer.
They placed the marquee where the light would fall across the tables like a held breath.
The cream canvas went up and made a new room out of air.
Indoors: sandwiches cut into architecture, lilies arriving in black buckets, a playlist her mother insisted was “background, not a statement.”
Sra. Serra appeared in the hall with earrings already on and the particular calm of a woman who had hosted well for twenty years.
“Laura, darling, the flags for the sandwiches—no, the other ones.
And do not let cook put the cream puffs near the window; the sun in Sarrià is a thief.”

It was then that Bosch’s man arrived with the pastry boxes and the news, spoken too casually for its weight: a man had been killed in the lane below—Soler, who lived in the narrow row of workers’ houses that the Serras’ guests never quite saw.
Horses, or a delivery van—accounts differed.
Dead. A widow.
Children.
The lane still smelling of the same morning.
Laura’s throat closed.
“We can’t possibly give a party,” she said.
“Not with a death—there—under us.”
José laughed, then stopped.
“Don’t be so extravagant.
People die every day.”
“I’m not extravagant.”
Laura’s voice shook.
“It’s—hideous.”
Sra. Serra, when told, did not pale.
She sat Laura on the bedroom chaise and held out a new hat—black ribbon, a soft brim that made Laura’s face look older and more decided.
“You are being absurd.
The party is arranged.
Those people would not expect us to stop living.
And look at yourself in the glass—my darling, you are too beautiful to ruin a morning for a man you never spoke to.”
The hat did something cruel and useful: it returned Laura to the surface of the day.
Guests arrived in quiet cars.
Champagne took the edge off the heat.
Someone praised the marquee.
Someone else filmed the lemon tree for a story that would vanish by evening.
Laura moved among them feeling strangely double—hostess and traitor—until Jordi found her by the roses and said she looked stunning, which was not the word she needed and was, for a moment, enough.
The party succeeded.
That was the horror of it.
It succeeded the way expensive things often succeed: without asking permission of the lane below.
When the last taxi door shut, Sra. Serra, flushed with triumph and fatigue, waved at the leftover cream puffs and sandwiches.
“Take them down to the Solers’, Laura.
It will be a kindness.
People like that appreciate a little attention.”
Laura walked down the path with the basket.
The air cooled between the pines.
The workers’ houses were closer than the villa’s windows admitted: laundry, a plastic chair, a door open on darkness.
A woman with swollen eyes took the basket without smiling.
Someone led Laura inside.
In the small front room a man lay on a bed as if listening.
The sheet was clean.
His face was young and remote, almost content, as if the accident had been a rumor about someone else.
Laura had expected horror.
Instead she found a quiet so complete that the party above seemed, suddenly, a noise made by children who did not know they were loud.
“Forgive my hat,” she whispered, absurdly, and did not know to whom.
Outside, Jordi was waiting at the turn of the path, hands in pockets, the city glittering behind him like a second party.
“Was it awful?” he asked.
Laura shook her head and then nodded.
Tears arrived without drama.
“It was—simply—so wonderfully—beautiful,” she tried, and could not finish the sentence into sense.
Jordi put his arm around her.
Above them, the marquee still glowed faintly among the trees, a pale room emptied of its occasion, holding nothing now but the evening and the knowledge she could not yet carry home.
